title: The burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6)
hook: a bush burns and is not consumed, and Moses turns aside to look
tomorrow: a name that is a verb

segments.voice: Yesterday, vayar: a prince who looked at his people's burdens, and ran for his life. Your line was he went out and saw. Now he's a shepherd in Midian, many years later. Day eighty-one.

Moses has a quiet life now. He married Tzipporah, one of the young women he helped at the well. He has a son. He works for his father-in-law, Jethro, keeping sheep. Years go by. The palace is a memory. One day he leads the flock deep into the wilderness, to a mountain called Horeb. Ordinary work, an ordinary day. Out of the corner of his eye, he sees a bush on fire. In the desert, dry brush catches. Plenty of people would keep walking. Today: hineni.
screen: `A SHEPHERD NOW, YEARS LATER.` → `AN ORDINARY DAY AT HOREB.` → `A BUSH ON FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's what makes it strange: "the bush was not consumed." It's burning, and it doesn't burn up. And Moses says: "I will turn aside now, and see this great sight, why the bush is not burnt." Then the verse that makes the whole story: "And when the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called unto him out of the midst of the bush." When God saw that he turned aside. Read it slowly. The call comes after Moses stops. It's as if the fire was burning for anyone who'd notice, and Moses was the one who did. Some teachers have pointed out that you'd only know the bush wasn't burning up if you watched it for a while. A glance wouldn't tell you. You'd have to stay. Then God calls: "Moses, Moses." And he answers: "Here am I." Hineni, the same word Abraham said. Then: don't come closer; "put off thy shoes from off thy feet, for the place whereon thou standest is holy ground." Ordinary dirt, on an ordinary mountain, where sheep had been grazing. The text calls it holy ground. And the call came on the day someone finally stopped. And why a thorn bush, a lowly desert plant? The midrash answers: to show that God is with the people in their suffering, in the thorns, not only in the cedars. A bush on fire that isn't destroyed. Some have read it as a picture of Israel itself, burning under slavery, and still there. Moses hides his face. He's afraid to look at God. He's about to find out why he was called.
screen: `THE BUSH WAS NOT CONSUMED.` · `I WILL TURN ASIDE NOW, AND SEE.` · `WHEN GOD SAW THAT HE TURNED ASIDE.` · `THIS IS HOLY GROUND.` · then, large: `HERE AM I.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn aside for one ordinary wonder. Settle, and breathe. Look around you, right where you are. Find one ordinary thing: light on a wall, the grain of a table, your own hand, a plant, a sound outside. Now do what Moses did. Turn aside. Stay with it longer than you normally would. Watch it the way you'd watch a fire that doesn't go out. What do you see now that you didn't see a minute ago? The bell holds the time.
Hineni, here am I, the word Moses answers with at the bush, the same word Abraham once said when God called him.
Your line: turn aside and see. Today, when something small catches your eye, don't walk past. Stop, and look a little longer. Day eighty-one.

screen: `DAY 81 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A NAME THAT IS A VERB.`

howItsDone: Jewish tradition reads the burning bush as the moment Moses is called, and teachers often use it to talk about noticing holiness in ordinary places; the Hebrew word for bush, sneh, is heard as an echo of Sinai.

fork.setup: you're a shepherd in the desert, far from anyone. out of the corner of your eye, a bush is on fire. what do you do?
options: run back to camp to warn people.
fork.reveal: Moses turns aside to see why the bush isn't burning up. only then does God call his name.

original.note: Hebrew: a thorn bush. the rabbis heard in it an echo of Sinai, the mountain to come.

trapdoor: what you thought: God got Moses's attention with a miracle.
what it means: the miracle was waiting for someone to stop. God calls when Moses turns aside.
what a scholar hears: sneh, a thorn bush. Exodus Rabbah 2:5: God chose a lowly thorn to show he suffers with Israel. some hear sneh as a pun on Sinai.

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Exodus 3:2–5, including 'Moses, Moses' and 'Here am I' (3:4).
The 'you'd have to watch it a while' idea is a modern teaching (often credited to Rabbi Lawrence Kushner); left unattributed as 'some teachers'. Confirm.
Exodus Rabbah 2:5 on the thorn bush: confirm.
sneh/Sinai pun: noted by commentators (e.g. Rashbam, Ibn Ezra?). Confirm attribution before naming anyone.
The reading of the bush as Israel under slavery is attributed to 'some'. Confirm.

Editor review: the narrator no longer states 'holy, because God is there' as fact (now 'the text calls it holy ground'); cut 'most people' and the superlative 'scrubbiest plant'; trapdoor 'many hear' softened to 'some'; added Exodus 2:21–23 as the source for Tzipporah, the son and the passing years.
